- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, reduce forecast overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to bullish sentiment.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤-0.5) and price is trending upward, adjust forecast downward by 3–7% to account for bearish sentiment drag.  
- When model forecast peaks sharply after a recent spike, reduce the peak by 5–15% to avoid overcorrection or “overshoot” bias.  
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., price drops after a spike), reduce forecasted highs by 5–10% in the following 5–7 days.  
- If sentiment history shows a recent reversal (e.g., from +1 to -1), adjust forecast to align with sentiment shift — e.g., if sentiment turns bearish, reduce forecast slope.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the first 5–7 days show strong upward movement, reduce forecasted peak by 5–10% to avoid overestimating short-term momentum.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.3), use historical mean reversion bias — forecast should not deviate more than ±3% from 14-day moving average.  
- If true outcome shows a sharp upward move after a low, reduce forecasted peak by 5–10% to avoid “lag” bias — model often overreacts to recent lows.
